notes.text: Note.— The muster roll of this Company was not reported in the Roll of Honor, and all my efforts thus far to procure a copy of it have proved abortive. I have reasons to hope that I may yet secure it, and if so will insert it at the end of this volume.

Note.— By a singular piece of goodfortune the roll of this company has reach- ed me, just as the press had reached the end of the regiment. I insert it at the wrong end as the best arrangement now possible under the circumstances.

notes.text: Note. — This roll was sent with the others of the same command and was marked Company A. This was evidently a mistake, as that company was given in another roll which corresponds with the record in the Roll of Honor. The companies of this regiment were designated in a curious way and so reversed all military rules that I supposed this must have been the missing roll of Com- pany C, and so have inserted it. It will be observed that it is a very imperfect record, and does not even give the name of the Captain.

notes.text: Note.— No story was ever more marred in the telling than the record of this regiment. I could find in North Carolina nothing but the roll of Battery A, in the "Roll of Honor" and the few names reported in Rumple's "History of Rowan," as belonging to Battery D. Not only half the men who went out with Capt. Reilly in 1861, but the remainder of the regiment were only to be found in the Archives Office in Washington. The reader will observe how miserably ex- ecuted were even these reports, originally sent to Richmond, but captured in 1865, and transferred to the Federal Capital. Not only were the casualties, but even the residences of the men omitted, and in this way there may be errors as to some of the homes attributed.

notes.text: Note.— No story was ever more marred in the telling than the record of this regiment. I could find in North Carolina nothing but the roll of Battery A, in the "Roll of Honor" and the few names reported in Rumple's "History of Rowan," as belonging to Battery D. Not only half the men who went out with Capt. Reilly in 1861, but the remainder of the regiment were only to be found in the Archives Office in Washington. The reader will observe how miserably ex- ecuted were even these reports, originally sent to Richmond, but captured in 1865, and transferred to the Federal Capital. Not only were the casualties, but even the residences of the men omitted, and in this way there may be errors as to some of the homes attributed.
